title: Eihei Dogen's Kindness and Compassion
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of integrating mindfulness and compassion into daily life, inspired by Dogen Zenji's teachings. By cultivating awareness and non-judgmental acceptance, one can bring clarity and peace to their inner state, effectively ending internal conflict. This approach encourages a universal awakening, where individual existence is seen as interconnected with others, fostering compassion and compassionate action in all aspects of life.

Through mindfulness and presence.

In Shobogenzo, the treasury of the true Dharma Eye, Dogen expounded upon profound Zen teachings, in a manner that became clear to me over time, Dogen addressed fundamental Buddhist concepts such as impermanence, emptiness, and the interconnectedness of all phenomena.
His skillful use of language and his ability to elucidate complex ideas and thoughts earned recognition as one of the greatest Buddhist philosophers.
We don't look at Shobogenzo as philosophy.
For us, it means something different, and what that is, is up to each one of us to find out.
There is a process, because I should say often I'm still totally lost and I have no idea what Dogen is saying.
But there's a process described by the Dogen scholar Stephen Heim that has been very helpful to me while studying Dogen.
It's called a hermeneutic loop.
I confess I had to look up what hermeneutic means.
It means concerning interpretation of texts like the Bible and, I guess, Shobogenzo.
But I took the liberty to take this out of his book, *Readings of Dogen's Treasury of the True Dharma Eye*, which, it's a great book.
I rewrote it a little and made it more compact.
So there are five steps to it.
One is the interpretive process.
The hermeneutic loop describes a dynamic process of interpretation and understanding.
It acknowledges that understanding Zen texts and teachings involves a continuous cycle of engagement between the scholar or student and the text that is being studied.
Two, there is a dialogue between you who is reading Dogen and the text.
According to Heim, the hermeneutic loop involves a back and forth interaction between us and the text.
We bring our own preconceptions, perspectives and intellectual framework to the interpretation process.
These things shape how we originally understand the text after the first reading.
Then comes step three, re-evaluation and re-interpretation.
We engage more deeply with the text and its cultural context as we become more familiar with it.
So there is a constant process of re-evaluation and re-interpretation.
New insights and understandings emerge through this ongoing dialogue.
Number four is integration of perspectives.
The hermeneutic loop involves integrating various perspectives, historical, cultural, linguistic, philosophical, into the interpretation.
It recognizes that the interpretation is never final or definitive, but is a provisional understanding that evolves with further study and reflection.
Sometimes that also means picking up some different translation and seeing what other people have to say when I'm really stuck.
It's actually kind of fun to see how that can play out.
Sometimes I doubt it's the same words that are translated.
Lots of head scratching is involved too.
Last but not least is the application to our Zen studies.
Heim applies the hermeneutic loop to navigate the complexities of studying the Shobogenzo.
It often presents rather paradoxical or enigmatic teachings.
Heim encourages us to engage deeply with the textual material while remaining aware of our own biases and assumptions.
This approach allows for a richer understanding of Zen philosophy and practice, historical development.
So Heim's concept underscores the dynamic nature of engaging with Zen texts.
It emphasizes the importance of flexibility, open-mindedness, and ongoing dialogue with the text.
That is what deepens our understanding of these teachings and their relevance.

I will only quote some selected commentaries because I don't want to bore you all too much with this work.

First, I'm going to read you Zheng Jiao's poem.
The text is as follows.
*The hub of Buddha's activity, the turning of the ancestors' hub, is known free of forms, illuminated beyond conditions.
As it is known free of forms, the knowledge is subtle.
As it is illuminated beyond conditions, the illumination is wondrous.
When the knowledge is subtle, there is no thought of discrimination.
When the illumination is wondrous, there is not the slightest hint.
Where there is no thought of discrimination, the knowledge is extraordinary with no comparison.
When there is not the slightest hint, the illumination has nothing to grasp.
The water is clear to the bottom where the fish swims without moving.
The sky is vast and boundless where the bird flies away and disappears.*
*The hub of Buddha's activity.
Buddhas do not fail to make Buddhas the hub.
The hub is manifested.
This is Zazen.
It is known free of forms.
This knowing is not, of course, conscious knowing.
Conscious knowing is small.
This knowing is not comprehension.
Comprehension is created.
Thus, this knowing is free of forms.
Being free of forms is this knowing.
Don't regard it as all-inclusive knowledge.
Don't limit it to self-knowledge.
Being free of forms is when brightness, duality, comes, meet it with brightness.
When darkness, non-duality, comes, meet it with darkness.
Sit through the skin you were born with.*
*Illuminated beyond conditions.
This illumination is not illuminating everything or illuminating with brilliance.
Being beyond condition is this illumination.
There is no thought of discrimination, means there is already merging.
There is already merging is actualization.
Thus, there is no thought of discrimination is not meeting even one person.*
Now, I could tell you more, but I need to leave some more stuff for you to explore on your own.
So now I will read you Dogen Zenchi's reinterpretation of this poem.
*The hub of Buddha's activity, the turning of the ancestor's hub, moves along with beyond thinking and is completed in the realm of beyond merging.
As it moves along beyond thinking, its appearing is immediate.
As it is completed in the realm beyond merging, completeness itself is realization.
When its appearing is intimate, you have no illusion.
When completeness reveals itself, it is neither real nor apparent.
When you have immediacy without illusion, immediacy is dropping away with no obstacles.
Realization, beyond real or apparent, is effort without expectation.
Clear water all the way to the bottom, a fish swims like a fish. [unclear: "Mass sky"] transparent throughout, a bird flies like a bird.*
And then, this is really cute actually, Dogen adds:
*Although Zenchiao's text is not incomplete, zazen may be spoken of in this way.
All descendants of Buddha ancestors should practice zazen as a single great matter.
It is the authentic seal transmitted from person to person.*
I love the practice realization brought forth.
Throughout Shobogenzo, Dogen emphasizes the inseparability of practice and realization, practice and enlightenment.
Realization is not something to be attained in the future.
It is now.
There is an emphasis on integrating Zen practice into everyday life.

It is manifested through ordinary activities and interactions, encouraging us all to see all aspects of life, whether in meditation, work, with our partners and husbands and children and wives, parents, as opportunities for awakening.
To this day, this perspective resonates deeply with me.
Compassion in some of the fascicles really provides practical examples and anecdotes that illustrate how compassion manifests in everyday life.

He advised the cook to treat each ingredient with care and respect.

Every mundane task treated like this is no longer mundane.
Dogen placed great emphasis on Sangha.
Our community is community throughout space and time.
He encouraged mutual support and care among his monks.
He believed that compassion should extend beyond individual concerns to encompass the well-being of the entire community.
This communal aspect of compassion is evident throughout Shobogenzo.
He responded to suffering.
He addressed the issue of suffering and how we should work with it.
He taught that when encountering suffering, whether within oneself or others, one should not turn away or ignore it, but instead face it directly with an open heart to become intimate with it.
This compassionate response involves listening deeply, offering support and taking action when possible to alleviate suffering and bring comfort.
What do I take away from all this?
I value practical acts of kindness as expressions of compassion.
Avalokiteshvara's compassion, hearing the cries of the world, joined together with Manjushri's wisdom.
And in that combination, they become Samantabhadra's helping hands, Samantabhadra's enlightening activity.

And none of it stays.
This too falls under the fleeting nature of impermanence.
We cannot get away from compassionate action.
It is life itself.
Let us not postpone our compassionate efforts.
Let's not postpone recognizing the impermanence of life and the opportunity to alleviate suffering in the present moment.
I'd like to end today's talk with a poem.
No, it's not by Dogen, and no, it's not even a Zen poem.
It doesn't actually have too much to do with today's talk.
I just like it a lot.
A life or death, you know, who is to say?
But I want to experience life and reality as long as I have the opportunity.
And this poem by Gina Poro, titled "Oh Death," really struck a chord with me.
*Death asked me to join him for dinner.
So I slipped into my favorite black dress that I had been saving for a special occasion and let him walk me to our [unclear: "candlelit chest"].
He ordered a ribeye extra rare.
I ordered two desserts and red wine.
And then I sipped and wondered why he looked so familiar and smelled like earth and memory.
He felt like a place both far away and deep within my body.
A place that whispers to me on the crisp autumn breeze along the liminal edges of dusk and dawn, somewhere between dancing and stillness.*
*He looked at me with the endless night sky in his eyes and asked, did you live your life, my love?
As I swirled my wine in its glass.
I wondered if I understood the thread I wove into the greater fabric.
If I loved in a way that was deep and freeing.
If I let pain and grief carve me into something more grateful.
If I made enough space to be in awe that flowers exist and take the time to watch the honeybees drink their sweet nectar.
I wondered what the riddles of regret and longing had taught me.
And if I realized just how beautiful and insignificant and monstrous and small we are.
For the brief moment that we are here before we all melt back down into the ancestors of the land.*
*[unclear: "Beth"] watched me lick buttercream from my fingers as he leaned in and said, my darling, it's time.
So I slipped my hand into his as he slowly walked me home.
I took a deep breath as he leaned in close for the long kiss goodnight.
And I felt a soft laugh escape my lips as his mouth met mine because I could never resist the man with the lust for my soul in his eyes and a kiss that makes my heart stop.*
If there was something in today's talk that is useful to you, please take it and make good use of it.
If I didn't, please forget every single word I said and return to our silence.
Thank you very much.
*May our intentions equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
I vowed Dharma is selfless.
I vowed to make then Buddha's way.
I vowed to come.*
